source: Kocsis & Szepesvari (2006) Bandit based Monte-Carlo planning
finding: UCT beats plain Monte Carlo and matches alpha-beta in convergence on random P-game trees. Failure rate = chance of picking a wrong move when stopped early.
numbers: Two tree shapes: branching 2 depth 20, and branching 8 depth 8. Each point averaged over 200 trees x 200 runs. UCT reaches zero failure in about the same leaf count as alpha-beta (order B^(D/2) iterations) and is faster if a small failure rate is accepted.
limits: Synthetic minimax trees with random move values in [0,127]; not real games. Alpha-beta assumed to guess randomly when unfinished. Bias term was changed from the proven form to a depth-decayed form for the experiments.
agent_relevance: Early-stop quality is the point: selective search gives usable answers at any budget, which fits an agent that must stop thinking at an arbitrary moment (control).

source: Kocsis & Szepesvari (2006) Bandit based Monte-Carlo planning
finding: Minimax-backup Monte Carlo (MMMC) was worse than plain MC at small budgets, so the bandit-driven selection, not the tree alone, produced the gain.
numbers: Figure 2: failure rate of MMMC higher than MC; MC plateaus at a significant failure level; UCT outperforms MC even at small searches.
limits: Read from figure description and text; no numeric table.
agent_relevance: Adding structure without a good selection rule can hurt. Tree plus bad exploration is not automatically better than flat sampling.

source: Kocsis & Szepesvari (2006) Bandit based Monte-Carlo planning
finding: Theory: with bias term scaled by the horizon D, the estimate bias is O(log n / n) and root failure probability goes to zero at a polynomial (not exponential) rate.
numbers: Theorem 6, finite-horizon MDP, rewards in [0,1], K actions per state. UCB1 constant Cp=1/sqrt(2).
limits: Polynomial rate is slow. Proof needs bounded rewards and drift conditions. The paper itself says stochastic shortest path (sailing) lies outside the theory.
agent_relevance: Guarantee is asymptotic only. With a few dozen LLM calls, theory says little; tuning of the exploration constant matters more.

source: Kocsis & Szepesvari (2006) Bandit based Monte-Carlo planning
finding: On the sailing MDP, UCT was tested against ARTDP and PG-ID. UCT needed a heuristic bias multiplier of 10; theory did not cover this domain.
numbers: Evaluation function = optimal value perturbed by up to +/-10%; 7 actions per state; error averaged over 1000 random states; episodes stopped with probability 1/Ns(t).
limits: Bias multiplier set by hand (upper bound on total reward). ARTDP used Boltzmann exploration tuned on small problems, so tuning is on both sides.
agent_relevance: The exploration constant is a hidden hand-tuned parameter. An LLM agent needs a scale for its value estimates before UCT-style balancing means anything.

source: Coulom (2006) Efficient Selectivity and Backup Operators in Monte-Carlo Tree Search
finding: Crazy Stone (9x9 Go) used a backup that moves from averaging to min-max as simulations grow, plus a selection rule that is not UCB. It won the 10th KGS computer-Go tournament.
numbers: 100-game matches, 95% CI: Crazy Stone (5 min) vs Indigo 2005 (8 min) 61% (+/-4.9). Vs GNU Go 3.6 level 10: 25% (+/-4.3) at 4 min, 32% (+/-4.7) at 8 min, 36% (+/-4.8) at 16 min per game.
limits: Only 9x9 Go; win rate vs GNU Go stayed below 50%. CIs of neighbouring time settings overlap.
agent_relevance: Search strength rises with thinking time (25% to 36% over 4x time). Averaging early and trusting the best later is a simple rule for how much to trust noisy estimates.

source: Coulom (2006) Efficient Selectivity and Backup Operators in Monte-Carlo Tree Search
finding: Coulom measured backup operators. The mean under-estimates a node and the max over-estimates it. Mean is better at few simulations, max at many; a mix that shifts from mean to robust-max is best across the range.
numbers: Table 1 mean squared error vs the value found with 2x the simulations: at 128 simulations mean 6.44, max 41.70, robust max 39.60, mix 5.29; at 131,072 simulations mean 2.84, max 1.83, robust max 1.88, mix 2.05.
limits: The reference value is itself computed with the Mix operator, so the test favours Mix. Go-specific; no independent replication in the paper.
agent_relevance: Average early, trust the best-looking branch only after many visits. A single high judge score from few samples should be discounted.

source: Silver et al. (2017) Mastering Chess and Shogi by Self-Play with a General RL Algorithm
finding: AlphaZero (MCTS plus a neural net, no handcrafted eval) beat the strongest alpha-beta engines in chess and shogi.
numbers: 100-game matches at one minute per move. Chess vs Stockfish: lost zero games. Shogi vs Elmo: lost eight. Beat Stockfish after 4 hours (300k steps) of training; 5,000 first-gen TPUs for self-play.
limits: Hardware (TPUs vs CPU engines) and engine settings were chosen by the authors; fairness was disputed in public commentary (not checked this session). Needs a perfect rules model and large training.
agent_relevance: MCTS wins when a learned value function is strong. Without a trained value model an LLM agent is not in this regime.

source: Silver et al. (2017) Mastering Chess and Shogi by Self-Play with a General RL Algorithm
finding: Search efficiency: AlphaZero evaluated far fewer positions yet scaled better with thinking time than alpha-beta.
numbers: About 80 thousand positions per second in chess and 40 thousand in shogi, versus 70 million for Stockfish and 35 million for Elmo.
limits: Elo scaling plot is relative to the engine at 40 ms; draws compress chess Elo. Result depends on network quality.
agent_relevance: Selective deep search with a good prior can replace brute breadth. For an LLM the prior is the model's own proposals: cheap but noisy.

source: Silver et al. (2017) Mastering Chess and Shogi by Self-Play with a General RL Algorithm
finding: Authors explain why averaging beats minimax with noisy learned values: MCTS averages over approximation errors so they cancel, while alpha-beta passes the largest error to the root.
numbers: Stated as an argument in the Methods; earlier MCTS chess programs without nets were much weaker than alpha-beta.
quote: MCTS averages over these approximation errors, which therefore tend to cancel out when evaluating a large subtree.
limits: Explanation is a hypothesis, not tested by an ablation in this paper.
agent_relevance: Reason to prefer averaged backup over best-child backup when value comes from an LLM judge with random error.

source: Schrittwieser et al. (2020) Mastering Atari, Go, Chess and Shogi by Planning with a Learned Model
finding: MuZero matches AlphaZero without being given the rules, and sets a state of the art on 57 Atari games, using MCTS over a learned model.
numbers: 800 simulations per move in board games, 50 in Atari. Reanalyze (re-running search on old data) reached 731% median normalised score vs 192%, 231%, 431% for earlier state-of-the-art.
limits: Atari needs huge training; the learned model predicts only reward, policy and value.
agent_relevance: Planning over a learned abstract model works. The LLM analogue is a model of consequences; errors there are the main risk.

source: Schrittwieser et al. (2020) Mastering Atari, Go, Chess and Shogi by Planning with a Learned Model
finding: Search matters for learning and for acting at low budgets: 6 simulations per move already gave a useful policy in Ms. Pacman; replacing search with model-free Q-learning matched R2D2 but learned slower and ended lower.
numbers: Ms. Pacman, 6 simulations per move (fewer than the number of actions) still improved quickly; more simulations jumped higher.
limits: Single game for this ablation; contrasts with earlier work that found small simulation counts weak.
agent_relevance: Tiny search budgets can help once value and policy are learned; the search signal is stronger than one-step targets.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: ToT (breadth-first, not MCTS) on Game of 24 with GPT-4 sharply beat chain of thought. This is the baseline LLM search result that MCTS papers compare with.
numbers: Success: IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC (k=100) 9.0%, ToT b=1 45%, ToT b=5 74%. Best of 100 CoT samples 49%, IO best of 100 33%.
limits: Not MCTS: fixed beam, no exploration bonus. One task family, 100 test items.
agent_relevance: Value of exploration is shown against a sample-matched baseline: 74% vs 49% at roughly equal sampling cost.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: Bottleneck is generation, not evaluation, and cost is high: ToT needs about as many tokens as 100 CoT trials.
numbers: GPT-3.5 ToT only 19% vs GPT-4 ToT 74%. GPT-4 generation + GPT-3.5 evaluation 64%; GPT-3.5 generation + GPT-4 evaluation 31%. ToT costs 5.5k completion tokens vs 6.7k for 100 CoT trials.
limits: Prompt changed from 1-shot to 3-shot for GPT-3.5 to make it work. Single cost comparison.
agent_relevance: A weak proposer cannot be rescued by a strong judge. Spend on proposal quality first.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP)
finding: RAP uses the LLM as both world model and policy with MCTS. On Blocksworld with LLaMA-33B it far outperformed CoT.
limits: Blocksworld has a clear checkable goal; reward uses the LLM's own state predictions. 6-step plans still only 26-42%. GPT-4 CoT is competitive at 6 steps (0.40 vs RAP(20) 0.42).
agent_relevance: MCTS lets a 33B model match or pass GPT-4 CoT on planning with only 20 iterations; deep plans remain hard.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP)
finding: On GSM8k and ProntoQA, gains from MCTS are smaller than on planning, and self-consistency is a strong rival.
numbers: GSM8k accuracy: CoT 29.4, CoT+SC(10) 46.8, Least-to-most 25.5 (42.5 with SC), RAP(1) 48.6, RAP(10) 51.6. ProntoQA: CoT 87.8 prediction / 64.8 proof; CoT+SC 89.8; RAP 94.2 / 78.8.
limits: RAP(1) 48.6 vs CoT+SC(10) 46.8 is close. Single seed; 33B open model.
agent_relevance: Much of the arithmetic gain comes from sampling plus aggregation; search adds a few points.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Language Agent Tree Search Unifies Reasoning, Acting, and Planning (LATS)
finding: LATS runs real MCTS with UCT, an LLM value, self-consistency and reflection. It set a code-generation record at publication.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1, 5 samples at expansion, 8 iterations: GPT-3.5 CoT 46.9, ReAct 56.9, Reflexion 68.1, ToT 54.4, RAP 63.1, LATS 83.8. GPT-4: base 80.1, Reflexion 91.0, LATS 92.7. MBPP (GPT-3.5): LATS 81.1 vs RAP 71.4.
limits: Uses real unit-test feedback and an environment that allows reverting; the GPT-4 gain over Reflexion is only +1.7. Costs more compute.
agent_relevance: Search plus an external checker gives the largest gains. At the top end the gain over simple retry is small.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Language Agent Tree Search Unifies Reasoning, Acting, and Planning (LATS)
finding: Ablation on HotPotQA: each component matters, and swapping MCTS for depth-first search loses a lot.
numbers: HotPotQA EM: ToT(ReAct) 0.39, RAP 0.54, LATS no LM heuristic 0.37, LATS DFS 0.42, LATS no reflection 0.58, full LATS 0.63. Best-of-250 ReAct 0.42; CoT-SC k=250 0.40; LATS n=1,k=50 0.48.
limits: Authors' own ablation. 'No LM heuristic' falling to 0.37 means the value function carries much of the gain. n=5 children, k=50 trajectories.
agent_relevance: Value quality matters at least as much as the select rule. 50 guided trajectories beat 250 unguided ones.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Language Agent Tree Search Unifies Reasoning, Acting, and Planning (LATS)
finding: Cost: LATS has the same sample complexity O(kn) as ToT and RAP and claims fewer nodes on success. Authors admit higher compute than simple prompting.
numbers: Table 9 tokens upon success: RAP 210,215; LATS 176,500 (second row 173,290; table layout ambiguous). At k=10: ToT 0.34 EM, RAP 0.44, LATS 0.44.
limits: Cost comparison only on HotPotQA; WebShop gains not cost-normalised. Hundreds of thousands of tokens per question.
agent_relevance: Budget check: a tree this size is costly. Use only when the question is hard and checkable.

source: Feng et al. (2023) Alphazero-like Tree-Search can Guide Large Language Model Decoding and Training (TS-LLM)
finding: Tree search with a learned value gave no big edge over simple breadth search on shallow problems but dominated on deep ones.
numbers: Path@1: GSM8k greedy 41.4, BFS-V 52.5, MCTS-alpha 51.9, MCTS-Rollout 47.8. Game24 greedy 12.7 vs 64.8 / 63.3 / 71.3. ProntoQA 48.8 greedy vs 94.4 / 99.4. Deep: chess endgame win rate 57.8 greedy vs 96.9 MCTS; RLHF reward 0.318 vs 2.221.
limits: MCTS-alpha is comparable to plain BFS on shallow tasks (depth 6-8). Needed trained value and outcome reward models.
agent_relevance: MCTS earns its cost only in deep, long-horizon problems; in shallow ones simple breadth search is enough.

source: Feng et al. (2023) Alphazero-like Tree-Search can Guide Large Language Model Decoding and Training (TS-LLM)
finding: Self-consistency beats tree search at equal tokens on small problems, and aggregation gains from search are smaller.
numbers: GSM8K: CoT-SC majority 46.8 vs CoT-SC with ORM 52.3, tree methods about 52. Authors: CoT-SC beats TS-LLM on GSM8k at equal token size because of its larger search space; tree-search aggregation benefits less.
limits: Tree search explores fewer distinct sentences (authors' cause). Authors call scalability of tree-search aggregation an open question.
agent_relevance: Parallel independent samples may beat a tree when the problem is short.

source: Feng et al. (2023) Alphazero-like Tree-Search can Guide Large Language Model Decoding and Training (TS-LLM)
finding: Training on search results improves policy and value (iterative update).
numbers: GSM8K MCTS accuracy: policy 0 value 0 = 51.9; after one round training both = 56.5; RFT baselines 47.0-47.5.
limits: Requires a training loop; not scaffold-only.
agent_relevance: Upper bound only; our agent does not train.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Lookahead search (a special case of MCTS without stochastic parts) underperformed beam search and best-of-N at equal generation budgets on MATH with a PRM. Compute-optimal allocation beat best-of-N with about 4x less compute.
numbers: Authors: 'lookahead-search generally underperforms other methods at the same generation budget'. A smaller model with extra test-time compute can beat a 14x larger model on easy and medium questions.
limits: PaLM 2-S* with a PRM; MATH only; they did not run full MCTS. They say rollouts spend budget and over-exploit the PRM.
agent_relevance: Deeper rollout estimates burn budget. Allocation by question difficulty matters more than the tree rule.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Search helps on hard questions but hurts on easy ones: the stronger optimiser over-exploits an imperfect verifier.
numbers: Beam search degrades relative to best-of-N on easy questions (levels 1-2) at high budgets but consistently beats best-of-N on levels 3-4. Budgets 4, 16, 64, 256 generations.
limits: Verifier is a learned PRM trained on MATH; effect tied to its error.
agent_relevance: Exploit only as hard as the judge is reliable. Add a difficulty gate: skip the tree for easy items.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Inference Scaling Laws: An Empirical Analysis of Compute-Optimal Inference for Problem-Solving with Language Models
finding: Direct compute-matched test: MCTS was worse than plain sampling at every budget on MATH with Llemma-7B and 34B, and was dropped from later comparisons.
numbers: Authors: MCTS 'underperforms the sampling-based methods at each compute budget, likely due to its costly rollouts'; MCTS often needs dozens of times more generated tokens. Llemma-7B needs about 2x fewer FLOPs than 34B for comparable accuracy.
limits: Their MCTS was a value-model rollout setup; later variants (rStar-Math) are stronger.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that vanilla MCTS can lose to cheaper methods. Compare any tree design with matched-token sampling.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Inference Scaling Laws: An Empirical Analysis of Compute-Optimal Inference for Problem-Solving with Language Models
finding: REBASE (a reward-balanced tree search with no UCT) was Pareto-optimal against sampling and MCTS.
numbers: With Llemma-7B, REBASE reached higher accuracy than sampling plus weighted voting with about 7 times less compute (Table 1).
limits: Table text garbled in extraction so no exact accuracy quoted; MATH500 and GSM8K only.
agent_relevance: A cheap tree that splits budget by reward is a better template than UCT rollouts.

source: Guan et al. (2025) rStar-Math: Small LLMs Can Master Math Reasoning with Self-Evolved Deep Thinking
finding: With MCTS plus a trained process preference model, 7B models reached o1-level math scores.
numbers: MATH pass@1 with 64 trajectories: Qwen2.5-Math-7B from 58.8% to 90.0%; Phi3-mini-3.8B 41.4% to 86.4% (o1-preview 85.5). AIME 2024: 53.3% (8/15), o1-mini 56.7. Omni-Math 50.5 vs o1-mini 60.5.
limits: Needs 4 rounds of self-evolution on 747k problems; geometry unsupported; no independent replication seen this session.
agent_relevance: Best MCTS result, but it depends on a trained step reward model, not on the tree rule.

source: Guan et al. (2025) rStar-Math: Small LLMs Can Master Math Reasoning with Self-Evolved Deep Thinking
finding: Ablation: MCTS with step rewards beats outcome-reward best-of-N, and returns saturate.
numbers: Table 8: ORM best-of-N MATH 82.6, AIME 26.7; PQM+MCTS 88.2/46.7; PPM+MCTS 89.4/50.0. With 4 trajectories it already beats Best-of-N baselines; MATH, AIME and Olympiad Bench saturate by 64 trajectories.
limits: PQM from raw Q-values struggled on hard benchmarks due to imprecise Q-values. Authors define the baselines.
agent_relevance: Step-level reward is the load-bearing part. Expect a plateau; do not scale budget past it.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) ReST-MCTS*: LLM Self-Training via Process Reward Guided Tree Search
finding: First iteration of tree search with a learned process reward did not beat self-consistency; only after repeated self-training did it.
numbers: MATH: after more self-training iterations 48.5% vs self-consistency 42.5% at matched sampling budget; iteration 1 'does not completely surpass' self-consistency.
limits: Qwen/Mistral-class 6-7B models; value trained on MCTS-derived labels.
agent_relevance: Tree search without a good value model is no better than voting.

source: Koh et al. (2024) Tree Search for Language Model Agents
finding: Best-first tree search in real web environments raised success of GPT-4o agents, and success grew with budget.
numbers: VisualWebArena (910 tasks): 39.7% relative gain, to 26.4% success. WebArena (812 tasks): 28.0% relative gain, to 19.2%. 200-task subset: baseline 24.5%; budget 5 expansions 32.0% (+30.6% rel.); budget 20 37.0% (+51%). Llama-3 text agent 7.6% to 10.1%.
limits: Best-first search, not UCT/MCTS. Up to 20x more LM calls; actions must be replayable. Depth 5, branching 5.
agent_relevance: Even a tiny budget of 5 gave most of the gain. Value function matters: LLaVA 30.0, GPT-4o 28.5 (no SC) / 32.5 (SC n=5).

source: Koh et al. (2024) Tree Search for Language Model Agents
finding: Depth and breadth must grow together; shallow or narrow trees give little.
limits: Subset of 200 tasks; sampling noise of a few points.
agent_relevance: Set breadth 3-5 and depth near the task horizon; gains per cost fall after the first few expansions.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1
finding: Failed attempt: the DeepSeek team tried AlphaGo-style MCTS to scale reasoning and gave it up for training. Majority voting still helped on top of long reasoning.
numbers: Reasons given: token search space is exponentially larger than chess; capping extensions per node led to local optima; a fine-grained value model is very hard to train. MCTS with a pre-trained value model still helped at inference. Majority voting lifted AIME 2024 from 79.8% to 86.7%.
limits: Negative result stated without numbers for the MCTS runs; one lab's report.
agent_relevance: Long single-chain reasoning plus voting beat tree search at scale. For a scaffold-only agent tree search is a niche tool, not the default.

source: Xie et al. (2024) Monte Carlo Tree Search Boosts Reasoning via Iterative Preference Learning
finding: MCTS-collected step preferences used for DPO training raised Mistral-7B scores.
numbers: GSM8K 81.8% (+5.9), MATH 34.7% (+5.8), ARC-C 76.4% (+15.8) over SFT. Ablation: step-level online 76.4 ARC-C vs offline variant 70.8 and instance-level 75.3.
limits: On MATH the gap between settings is small (32.2 vs 29.0 without ground truth). Training required.
agent_relevance: Search used as a data generator, not at test time.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Rival to tree search: plain repeated sampling raises coverage log-linearly, but selecting the right answer plateaus without a verifier.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250 samples (single-sample SOTA 43%). Without automatic verifiers, majority vote and reward models plateau beyond several hundred samples.
limits: Only the abstract and introduction were read closely; needs automatic verification for the gain to be real.
agent_relevance: The baseline any tree design must beat at equal tokens. With a checker, sampling plus verify is hard to beat.
